When I last checked Google's privacy policy it was written so widely that Google could, in principle, record absolutely everything you do online. There are actually two different privacy policies, one for Chrome and one for the use of other Google services, and they have been written very elegantly (I imagine a team of very smart lawyers made a lot of money on this) so as to allow Google almost unlimited latitude, whilst appearing superficially to be moderately reasonable. Clearly Chrome can't listen in when the computer is turned off, and I imagine that if you have closed the program it is no longer capable of listening (though you should check this with an expert, as some programs - Skype, for example - do not fully "close" when you sign out of them, and I'm not sure how things work with the most recent Chrome release). The key point is that there is nothing in the two agreements to stop Google from logging all your activity on Chrome (all the sites you visit, your IP address, your physical location, etc.) - a statement that Google will not do this is conspicuous by its absence - and there is nothing to stop Google from linking this activity to your real-world identity, insofar as they can determine it. Google's privacy policy is a little masterpiece of legal obfuscation, and you should be very careful when using any Google service or software.
